23647: God is infinite, all-knowing and cannot be tempted; humans are finite, learn and can be tempted. How can one person be both without being a hybrid, a split personality, or one nature disguised as the other?
23648: Chalcedonian Christology: two natures, one person
23649: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and most Protestant churches; Pope Leo I's *Tome*; the Council of Chalcedon (451)
23650: Jesus is one person (the eternal Son) who has two complete natures, divine and human, 'without confusion, change, division or separation'. Whatever is true of either nature is true of the one person, so one can say 'God was born' or 'the man Jesus is Lord'. The infinite is not shrunk; the Son takes a full human nature into union with himself.
23652: Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac); following Cyril of Alexandria's formula 'one incarnate nature of God the Word'
23653: After the union, Christ has one nature that is fully divine and fully human, without mixture or loss. Oriental Orthodox churches rejected Chalcedon's wording but not its intent; modern dialogues (e.g. statements in 1989-1990 between Eastern and Oriental Orthodox) concluded the disagreement is largely about terminology.
23655: Gottfried Thomasius, P. T. Forsyth, some modern evangelicals and others
23656: Based on Philippians 2:7 ('emptied himself'), the Son voluntarily set aside the use (or in stronger versions, the possession) of some divine attributes such as omniscience during his earthly life. This explains his growth and limitations. Critics say strong kenosis implies God stops being God; moderate versions speak only of restraint in use.
23657: Rejected options that drop a pole
23658: Arianism (Son a created being), Docetism (only seemed human), Apollinarianism (no human mind), Nestorianism (two persons), Eutychianism (natures blended)
23659: These were judged heresies precisely because each removed the tension by shrinking one side. Their history helps explain why the mainstream wording is so careful. Some historians argue Nestorius himself was closer to orthodoxy than his opponents portrayed, a debated point.
23660: Being omniscient and not omniscient, immortal and mortal, are contradictory properties. No one can have both.
23661: The classical claim is that one person has them in respect of different natures: the Son is omniscient as God and learns as man. Philosophers (e.g. Thomas Morris, Oliver Crisp) have offered models such as a 'two-minds' view to show this is not formally contradictory. Whether it is true is a matter of faith and evidence; whether it is coherent has defenders in professional philosophy.
23662: Because Jesus is human, he sympathizes with weakness and temptation; because he is God, he can actually save. Many Christians draw comfort from both in prayer.
23663: Jesus knows all things, yet does not know the day
23664: Peter says to the risen Jesus, 'Lord, you know everything', and the disciples say the same earlier. Yet Jesus himself says no one knows the day or hour of the end, not even the Son, but only the Father.
23665: The Gospels portray Jesus with real divine insight and real human limits, and traditions explain the limit in different ways.
23667: Peter says, 'Lord, you know everything.' The disciples say, 'now we know that you know all things.' Jesus knew what was in people. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
23668: He does not know the day
23669: Concerning that day or hour, no one knows, not the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. He grew in wisdom. He asked who touched him.
23670: If Jesus is God, he knows everything, including the date of his return. If he does not know it, how is he God, and how did the disciples say he knew all things?
23671: Two natures: ignorant as man, omniscient as God
23672: Athanasius, Gregory of Nazianzus, Leo I and most Chalcedonian theologians
23673: Jesus speaks here from his human mind, which genuinely learned and had limits. As the divine Son he knows all things. Mark 13:32 is about what the incarnate Son knew in his human consciousness, not about the eternal Son's knowledge.
23675: Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, and others in the Latin tradition
23676: The phrase means the Son does not know it in a way he was sent to make known; it was not part of his revealing mission. Critics think this strains the plain sense; defenders note similar idioms of 'knowing' and point to Acts 1:7, where the times are set by the Father's authority.
23678: Kenotic theologians and many modern evangelicals
23679: In becoming human, the Son voluntarily did not exercise his divine omniscience, depending instead on the Spirit and the Father for what he needed to know. The disciples' 'you know all things' refers to his remarkable, Spirit-given knowledge of people and events, and after the resurrection to his glorified state.
23680: Mark 13:32 shows the earliest Christians did not think Jesus was God; later church writers had to explain it away.
23681: Mark's Gospel also has Jesus forgive sins in a way the scribes call blasphemy and claim to be the one who will come on the clouds. Critical scholars do often regard this saying as authentic precisely because it is awkward, and it shows that the early church preserved hard sayings. Whether it fits a high Christology depends on the two-natures framework, which has been the mainstream answer since the fourth century.
23682: Jesus' own refusal to name the date stands against all date-setting for the end. Christians are called to watch and be ready, not calculate.
23683: The Father is greater, yet the Son and Father are one
23684: Jesus says, 'I and the Father are one', and his hearers take it as a claim to deity. He also says, 'the Father is greater than I', and that he does only what he sees the Father doing. Christians have long debated how these fit.
23685: The Son is equal with the Father in being, while gladly receiving and obeying the Father, at least in his earthly mission.
23687: I and the Father are one. Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. He was making himself equal with God. Before the world existed he shared the Father's glory.
23689: The Father is greater than I. The Son can do nothing of himself. The head of Christ is God. In the end the Son himself will be subject to the Father.
23690: If the Father is greater, is the Son less than fully God? If they are one and equal, what does 'greater' mean?
23692: Athanasius, Augustine, and much of the Latin and Reformed tradition
23693: As God the Son is equal; as the man who took the form of a servant he is less. John 14:28 speaks from his incarnate state on the eve of the cross, which is why it is linked to his going to the Father.
23694: Monarchy of the Father: greater as source, not in being
23695: Gregory of Nazianzus and the Eastern Orthodox tradition; also some Western writers
23696: The Father is 'greater' as the eternal source from whom the Son is begotten, not as superior in nature. A son is equal in humanity to his father yet comes from him. This order of origin is eternal and does not make the Son less God.
23698: Some contemporary evangelicals (e.g. Wayne Grudem, Bruce Ware); strongly opposed by others (e.g. Kevin Giles, Millard Erickson, many Reformed classical theists)
23699: Advocates hold that the Son is equal in being but eternally submits to the Father's authority, citing 1 Corinthians 15:28. Opponents argue that an eternal difference in authority implies a difference of will and so of nature, departing from Nicene orthodoxy. This intra-evangelical debate intensified around 2016.
23701: Arius; modern Unitarians and Jehovah's Witnesses
23702: The Father alone is true God and the Son is the highest created being. This resolves the tension by dropping full deity. Nicene Christians reply that 'I and the Father are one' and the worship of Jesus cannot be fitted to a created Son.
23703: Jesus plainly said the Father is greater. Trinitarians must twist that into meaning nothing.
23704: Every serious Trinitarian reading takes the verse as meaning something real: subordination in the incarnation, or order of origin. The same Gospel also records claims that hearers treated as making himself equal to God. Any reading has to account for both, so the question is which account handles all of John best.
23705: Jesus' joyful dependence on the Father is presented as the model for Christian life: equal dignity does not rule out glad submission and love.
23706: Christ died, yet God cannot die
23707: Scripture says God alone has immortality, and God is from everlasting to everlasting. Yet it also says people 'crucified the Lord of glory' and that God bought the church 'with his own blood'. If Jesus is God and Jesus died, did God die?
23708: The eternal Son truly died in his human nature, while the divine nature itself did not cease to exist.
23710: God alone has immortality. He is from everlasting to everlasting. He is the immortal, invisible God.
23712: They crucified the Lord of glory. They killed the Author of life. God obtained the church with his own blood. Christ died for our sins.
23713: If Jesus is God and Jesus died, God died, which contradicts his immortality. If God did not die, was it only a man who died, and was the death then less than divine?
23715: Cyril of Alexandria, Council of Ephesus (431), Second Council of Constantinople (553), and Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed theology in varying forms
23716: What happens to either nature is truly said of the one person. The Son of God died, in his human nature: his human soul and body separated, while his divine nature, which cannot die, remained united to both. So it is right to say 'one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh' without saying that the divine nature ceased.
23718: Common across the Fathers and later theologians
23719: In scripture, death is separation, not ceasing to exist. Jesus' body lay in the tomb and his spirit went to the Father. Death meant the Son entering fully into the human experience of death, not God going out of existence.
23721: Martin Luther (in his stronger statements), Jürgen Moltmann (*The Crucified God*), many modern theologians
23722: The cross reveals that God himself enters suffering and death, and Christian thought should let this reshape the doctrine that God cannot suffer (impassibility). Classical theists answer that this risks making God subject to change and loss; defenders say the cross must reveal God's heart, not just a human nature's experience.
23723: If God can't die, then the death on the cross was a mere human death. If God did die, who ran the universe for three days?
23724: The traditional answer is that the person who died was divine, so the death was not 'mere', but the divine nature did not stop; the Son remained God throughout, upholding all things. The 'who ran the universe' question assumes God's nature ceased, which no mainstream tradition teaches.
23725: Christian worship speaks of the love of a God who went as far as death for people. The paradox also shapes how believers think about their own death: as something Christ has passed through, not an annihilation.
23726: Prince of peace, yet came to bring a sword
23727: Angels announce peace on earth at Jesus' birth, and he leaves his peace with his followers. Yet Jesus says he did not come to bring peace but a sword, setting family members against each other.
23728: Jesus brings peace with God and between enemies, but loyalty to him divides people who reject him from those who follow.
23729: Peace on earth among those with whom he is pleased. My peace I give to you. He is our peace, who broke down the dividing wall. Blessed are the peacemakers.
23730: Do not think I came to bring peace on earth; I came not to bring peace but a sword. A person's enemies will be those of his own household.
23731: Is Jesus a peacemaker or a divider? Did he come to end conflict or to cause it?
23733: Most commentators, e.g. John Chrysostom, John Calvin, modern evangelical and Catholic scholars
23734: The 'sword' is the result of his coming, not its goal. People who follow Jesus are often rejected by those closest to them, as Micah 7:6 foresaw. Luke's parallel says 'division' rather than 'sword'. The peace he gives is real but does not compel everyone to accept it.
23735: Peace with God now, full peace later
23737: The peace Jesus brings first is reconciliation with God and between believers. Universal peace on earth awaits the end. Until then, his kingdom provokes opposition. Luke 2:14 itself limits peace to 'those with whom he is pleased'.
23738: The sword is not a weapon for disciples
23739: Anabaptist and Mennonite traditions, Quakers, and many pacifist readers; also mainstream exegetes
23740: Whatever the sword means, Jesus forbids his followers to use it for his cause: he tells Peter to put away his sword. The 'sword' elsewhere is God's word that cuts. So Matthew 10:34 cannot justify Christian violence; it describes suffering disciples, not violent ones.
23741: Jesus admits he came to bring a sword, and Christians have used this to justify religious violence for centuries.
23742: The context is about family division because of loyalty to him, and in the same Gospel he blesses peacemakers and rebukes Peter's sword. Most interpreters from the Fathers to today read the sword as division suffered, not violence inflicted. Christians have indeed misused texts to justify violence, which this passage does not support when read in context.
23743: Christians are called to seek peace with everyone as far as it depends on them, while accepting that following Jesus may cost relationships. The aim is to be peacemakers, not to provoke division needlessly.
23744: Came not to judge, yet the judge of all
23745: In John's Gospel Jesus says God did not send the Son to condemn the world but to save it, and that he does not judge anyone who hears and does not keep his words. In the same Gospel he says the Father has given all judgement to the Son and that he came into the world for judgement.
23746: Jesus' first coming aims at saving, yet his very presence exposes people, and he will be the final judge.
23748: God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save it. I do not judge him; I did not come to judge the world but to save it. I judge no one.
23750: The Father judges no one but has given all judgement to the Son. For judgement I came into this world. God has fixed a day to judge the world by the man he appointed.
23751: Did Jesus come to judge or not? John records both claims, sometimes in the same chapter.
23753: Augustine, John Calvin, and most commentators on John
23754: His purpose was to save, but the light inevitably exposes. John 3:18-19 explains: the one who does not believe is condemned already, and the judgement is that light came and people loved darkness. Judgement is the shadow cast by rejected salvation.
23757: The first coming is for salvation; the second coming is for judgement. 'I did not come to judge' describes his earthly mission; 'all judgement is given to the Son' describes his role at the end.
23758: His word judges; he judges as the Saviour
23759: Some contemporary theologians, e.g. Karl Barth's 'Judge judged in our place', and restorative-justice readings
23760: John 12:48 says the word Jesus spoke will judge on the last day. The judge is the same one who was judged in our place, so judgement is in the hands of the one most committed to saving. Critics warn this can soften real condemnation; defenders say it shows what kind of judge he is.
23761: John's Jesus contradicts himself on the most basic question of his mission.
23762: John places these sayings close together, and in John 3 explains the link directly: rejection of the light is itself the judgement. Writers who include both, side by side, are making a point about the double effect of light, not overlooking a slip.
23763: Believers can approach Jesus without fear of condemnation, since he came to save. At the same time, his words are not optional; they are the standard by which life will be weighed.
23764: Justified by faith, not by works, yet by works and not by faith alone
23765: Paul says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Both use Abraham as their example, which makes the contrast sharper.
23766: Paul and James both reject a dead faith and a self-earned salvation; they mostly use 'faith', 'works' and 'justify' in different senses.
23768: A person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. To the one who does not work but trusts God, faith is counted as righteousness. By grace you have been saved through faith, not by works.
23770: A person is justified by works and not by faith alone. Faith without works is dead. Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac, and faith was completed by works.
23771: James 2:24 says 'not by faith alone', the very phrase the Reformation used to sum up Paul. Are the two apostles in conflict about how a person is put right with God?
23773: John Calvin, most Reformed, Lutheran and evangelical scholars (Luther himself was famously uneasy with James)
23774: Paul's 'works of the law' are deeds offered to earn standing with God; James's 'works' are the fruit of living faith. Paul's 'justify' means declared righteous before God; James's 'justify' means shown to be righteous, vindicated. Paul fights legalism; James fights empty profession. Faith alone saves, but the faith that saves is never alone.
23776: Roman Catholic Church (Council of Trent, Session 6, 1547); Thomas Aquinas
23777: Justification is God's work of making a person righteous, begun in baptism by grace, not earned. Saving faith is faith 'formed by love', so good works done in grace genuinely cooperate in growth in justification and merit reward, though always as God's gift. James 2:24 is read at face value; Paul excludes works done apart from grace, especially works of the Mosaic law.
23780: Salvation is not mainly a legal verdict but union with God, a lifelong healing in which grace and human cooperation work together. Faith and works are not rival grounds of salvation but two sides of participating in God's life. The Western debate is seen as somewhat foreign to the categories of the Greek Fathers.
23781: E. P. Sanders, James Dunn, N. T. Wright and others (with significant variations)
23782: Paul's 'works of the law' mainly means Jewish boundary markers such as circumcision, food laws and Sabbath that separated Jews from Gentiles. Paul argues Gentiles belong to God's people by faith without becoming Jews; he is not arguing against good deeds. On this reading Paul and James address different questions and do not collide.
23783: James was written to refute Paul, and the two cannot both be inspired.
23784: Some scholars do think James responds to a distorted form of Pauline teaching, but even they usually note that James's target, a faith that says 'be warm and filled' while ignoring the hungry, is something Paul also condemns. Paul himself insists on faith working through love and on judgement according to deeds. The vocabulary clashes; the underlying concerns overlap considerably.
23785: Christians across traditions agree that genuine faith shows itself in love and action, and that no one earns God's favour by good deeds. The disagreements are about the exact relationship, which affects how believers think about assurance and confession.
23786: Already saved, yet still to be saved
23787: Paul tells the Ephesians 'by grace you have been saved'. He tells the Romans their salvation is nearer now than when they first believed, and the Philippians to work out their salvation with fear and trembling. Salvation is spoken of as past, present and future.
23788: Salvation is a done deal, an ongoing process and a future hope all at once.
23790: By grace you have been saved. He saved us by the washing of regeneration. There is now no condemnation for those in Christ.
23792: Salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. In hope we were saved. We wait for the redemption of our bodies.
23793: If believers are already saved, what remains? If salvation is still future, how can they be sure they have it?
23794: Inaugurated eschatology: the already and the not yet
23795: Widely held across traditions; associated with scholars such as Geerhardus Vos, Oscar Cullmann and George Eldon Ladd
23796: God's future has broken into the present in Jesus, but is not yet complete. Believers are already forgiven and given the Spirit as a down payment; they will be fully saved, bodies included, when Christ returns. Both statements are true at different points on the same timeline.
23798: Common in evangelical and Reformed teaching
23799: I have been saved from sin's penalty (justification), I am being saved from sin's power (sanctification), and I will be saved from sin's presence (glorification). Paul uses 'saved' for all three, which explains the different tenses.
23800: Salvation as a journey of healing
23801: Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic and Wesleyan emphases on growth
23802: Salvation is a living relationship and lifelong process of healing, begun in baptism and faith, continued through perseverance, and completed at the resurrection. The 'already' is real, but it can be neglected; the 'not yet' requires ongoing cooperation with grace.
23803: Christians can't decide whether they are saved or not, so they redefine 'saved' whenever it suits them.
23804: The variation is in the texts themselves and follows a consistent pattern: the past tense refers to what God has done in Christ, the future to the resurrection and final judgement. Many future-oriented belief systems talk this way, as in 'we have won the war but the last battle is still to come'.
23805: Believers can live with settled security and with serious effort at the same time, without either complacency or anxiety. It also explains why Christian life still includes struggle.
23806: God chooses, yet we must preach and persuade
23807: Paul speaks of God choosing people before the foundation of the world, and Jesus says no one can come to him unless the Father draws them. Yet the same Paul pleads with people, travels thousands of miles and says people cannot believe unless someone preaches.
23808: Scripture uses election as a reason for mission, not a reason to stop.
23810: He chose us in him before the foundation of the world. No one can come to me unless the Father draws him. As many as were appointed to eternal life believed.
23812: Go and make disciples of all nations. How will they believe without someone preaching? I have become all things to all people that by all means I might save some. We implore you, be reconciled to God.
23813: If God has already chosen who will be saved, why does evangelism matter? If it matters, does human effort decide who is saved?
23814: God ordains the means as well as the end
23815: Reformed and Calvinist theology, e.g. Charles Spurgeon, William Carey, J. I. Packer (*Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God*)
23816: The God who chose people also chose to save them through the preaching of the gospel. Election guarantees that evangelism will bear fruit. Paul endures everything 'for the sake of the elect', and God tells him in Corinth to keep preaching because 'I have many people in this city'.
23818: Arminian, Wesleyan and many Pentecostal and Baptist believers
23819: God elects those he foreknows will believe, or he elects Christ and all who are in him. Preaching gives each hearer a real opportunity to respond, so the outcome of evangelism is genuinely open. This makes urgency natural.
23821: Many biblical scholars (e.g. N. T. Wright), and Karl Barth in a different form
23822: In scripture election is often a calling to a people for the sake of others, as Abraham was chosen so that all nations would be blessed. Being chosen is not mainly about who goes to heaven but about being sent. Election and mission are then the same thing seen from two sides.
